cls: Antimalarial - biguanide dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor (causal prophylactic)
pharm: Prodrug metabolised to cycloguanil, which inhibits plasmodial dihydrofolate reductase, blocking folate synthesis and parasite nucleic-acid replication, including the liver (pre-erythrocytic) stage
tags: Malaria prophylaxis (with chloroquine, or as atovaquone-proguanil)
quick: Prophylaxis 200 mg once daily (often with chloroquine); start before travel, continue 4 weeks after
Take after food, at the same time each day; doses by weight in children
Considered safe with folate supplementation; useful where chloroquine-sensitive
Small amounts in milk; the infant still needs its own malaria prophylaxis
Reduce dose/frequency in renal impairment (cycloguanil accumulates)
Use with caution; activation to cycloguanil is hepatic
Adherence, mouth ulcers, blood counts with prolonged use; renal function
summary: Proguanil is a biguanide antimalarial used mainly for the prophylaxis of malaria. It is a prodrug converted in the body (chiefly by CYP2C19) to the active metabolite cycloguanil, a selective inhibitor of plasmodial dihydrofolate reductase; by blocking folate synthesis it prevents the parasite from making nucleic acids and proteins, acting on both the pre-erythrocytic (liver) and blood stages. For prophylaxis the adult dose is 200 mg once daily, classically taken together with weekly chloroquine in areas of chloroquine-sensitive or low-resistance malaria; it is started 1-2 days before entering the malarious area and continued for 4 weeks after leaving. Proguanil is also a fixed-dose component of atovaquone-proguanil (a widely used prophylactic and treatment combination). Proguanil as a single agent is not FDA-approved, so dosing follows the BNF, WHO and other national malaria guidance. It is well tolerated, with mild gastrointestinal effects and mouth ulcers being the commonest problems; the dose must be reduced in renal impairment, and folate supplementation is given in pregnancy.

moa: Proguanil is a biguanide prodrug. It is metabolised (mainly by hepatic CYP2C19) to cycloguanil, a potent and selective inhibitor of plasmodial dihydrofolate reductase. Inhibiting this enzyme blocks the reduction of folate to tetrahydrofolate, halting synthesis of thymidylate and ultimately of the parasite's DNA, RNA and proteins. This stops development of the pre-erythrocytic (liver) forms and the asexual blood stages. Proguanil also has intrinsic activity (independent of cycloguanil) that synergises with atovaquone by collapsing the parasite mitochondrial membrane potential, which is the basis of the atovaquone-proguanil combination.

relative: Severe renal impairment (reduce dose; risk of cycloguanil accumulation and haematological toxicity)
monitor: Adherence with the full pre- and post-travel course
Full blood count with prolonged or high-dose use, especially in renal impairment

preg: Proguanil is considered one of the safer antimalarials in pregnancy and may be used (typically with chloroquine) where the parasites are sensitive. Because it inhibits folate metabolism, give folic acid supplementation (e.g. 5 mg daily) during pregnancy.
lact: Small amounts of proguanil are excreted in breast milk - too little to protect the infant. A breastfed infant who needs protection must receive its own appropriate malaria prophylaxis; the amount in milk is not considered harmful.
renal: Proguanil and its active metabolite cycloguanil are renally eliminated and accumulate in renal impairment, increasing the risk of haematological toxicity (megaloblastic changes, pancytopenia). Reduce the dose and/or dosing interval according to creatinine clearance; avoid or use with great caution in severe impairment.
hepatic: Proguanil is activated to cycloguanil by the liver; use with caution in hepatic impairment, and note that activation may be reduced.

major: Warfarin and other coumarin anticoagulants - proguanil can enhance the anticoagulant effect (monitor INR)
moderate: Other folate antagonists (e.g. co-trimoxazole, methotrexate, pyrimethamine) - additive antifolate/haematological toxicity
CYP2C19 inhibitors (e.g. omeprazole, fluvoxamine) - may reduce conversion to active cycloguanil
Antacids/magnesium-containing preparations - reduce proguanil absorption (separate dosing)
minor: Other antimalarials - generally combined intentionally (e.g. chloroquine, atovaquone)
interactions.food: Take after food; avoid taking with antacids/magnesium salts at the same time
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; observe sensible limits
interactions.diagnostics: May enhance warfarin effect (monitor INR); monitor full blood count and renal function with prolonged use

serious: Megaloblastic anaemia and pancytopenia (mainly with renal impairment or overdose)
rare: Skin reactions including hair loss and scaling

monitoring: Adherence to the full prophylactic course (before travel and 4 weeks after)
Full blood count with prolonged or high-dose use, particularly in renal impairment
Renal function; INR if on warfarin
counsel: This medicine helps prevent malaria - take it every day at the same time, with food, exactly as directed
Start it before you travel and keep taking it for 4 weeks after you return, even when you feel well
Still protect yourself from mosquito bites (repellent, nets, covering up) - no tablet is 100% effective
Tell your doctor if you get mouth ulcers, easy bruising or bleeding, or if you have kidney problems or take warfarin
If you develop fever during or after travel, seek medical attention and mention you were in a malaria area
pk: Acts on liver and blood stages; prophylaxis requires dosing started before exposure
Plasma peak about 2-4 hours after an oral dose
Elimination half-life about 12-20 hours (prolonged in renal impairment)
Once-daily dosing; prophylaxis continued for 4 weeks after leaving the malarious area
Store at controlled room temperature, protect from moisture
pearls: Prodrug activated (CYP2C19) to cycloguanil - inhibits plasmodial dihydrofolate reductase; acts on liver and blood stages
Classic prophylaxis is proguanil 200 mg daily plus weekly chloroquine; also the proguanil half of atovaquone-proguanil
Proguanil-alone is not FDA-approved - dosing follows BNF/WHO. Reduce dose in renal impairment (cycloguanil accumulates)
Safe in pregnancy with folate supplementation; separate from antacids/magnesium which reduce absorption
Continue prophylaxis for 4 weeks after leaving the area and maintain bite-avoidance measures
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day; if it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed one - do not double up. Consistent daily dosing is important for protection, so resume your usual schedule and complete the full course.
overdose: Proguanil has a wide safety margin, but large overdoses (especially with renal impairment) can cause epigastric discomfort, vomiting, haematuria and reversible haematological effects (megaloblastic changes). There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with monitoring of blood counts and renal function. Folinic acid may be considered for marked antifolate haematological toxicity.
